work: Le Lézard aux plumes d’or (The Lizard with Golden Feathers)
story: Joan Miró wrote an original surrealist poem and collaborated with publisher Louis Broder to produce a suite pairing his handwritten verses with lithographs, originally planned for release in 1967 [sothebys.com, pamono.com]. After printing the initial run, Miró and Broder discovered that a defect in the paper factory had caused an alteration of the colors [pamono.com]. Because the original lithographic plates had already been erased before the flaw was detected, the entire first edition had to be abandoned [christies.com, pamono.com]. Miró was forced to create an entirely new series of plates from scratch, delaying the project's final publication until 1971 [christies.com, pamono.com].

Art dealer Léonce Rosenberg originally initiated this collaborative project between painter Juan Gris and poet Pierre Reverdy during World War I, with sources dating its start to 1915, 1916, or 1917. The original plan paired one of Gris's plates with each of Reverdy's twenty poems, but work halted when Gris died of kidney failure in 1927 at age forty, leaving only eleven lithographs finished. Nearly thirty years after Gris's death, the publisher Tériade revived the stalled undertaking alongside Reverdy. The resulting book was finally published in 1955 containing the twenty poems accompanied by Gris's completed prints as a tribute to the late artist.

Sigmund Freud published his final book, *Moses and Monotheism*, in 1939, arguing that Moses was born into Egyptian nobility rather than Hebrew heritage. Decades later, Salvador Dalí illustrated the text by drawing directly onto massive gold plates with a diamond-tipped stylus. The resulting engravings were printed in color on lambskin. Dalí paired Freud’s historical psychoanalysis with his own nonsensical foreword, baffling readers with bizarre references to Confucius and the Perpignan train station.
